Multi-scale Spatial Autocorrelation Analysis

Source: R/multi_scale_ac.R
multiScaleAC.Rd

Computes bivariate Moran's I across a range of kernel bandwidths, producing a functional curve \(I(h)\) rather than a single value at one chosen scale. Inference is by permutation of the second gene.

multiScaleAC(
  coords,
  gene1,
  gene2,
  h,
  ...,
  perms = 1000,
  seed = 333,
  eps = 0,
  nan_policy = c("zero", "drop", "na"),
  moments = TRUE,
  permute = c("all", "flagged", "none"),
  batch_size = 256,
  n_threads = 0,
  verbose = NULL,
  large_mode_n = NULL,
  kernel = c("gaussian", "uniform", "exponential"),
  distance = c("euclidean", "manhattan", "minkowski")
)

Arguments

coords

numeric matrix of spatial coordinates (N x 2)

gene1

numeric vector of expression values for the first variable (length N)

gene2

numeric vector of expression values for the second variable (length N)

h

numeric vector of kernel bandwidths, in the same units as coords (must be > 0). See the bandwidth section below; choosing these on the wrong scale is the most common way to get a meaningless result.

...

additional parameters forwarded to the distance and kernel functions, and p for the built-in Minkowski distance. Note that ... precedes every option in the signature, so options must be named exactly; that is what stops a parameter such as p from being partially matched against one of them.

perms

integer number of permutations (default: 1000). 0 is permitted and returns the observed curve with no permutation matrix.

seed

integer random seed for reproducibility (default: 333)

eps

numeric weight threshold (default: 0, meaning no thresholding). Weights are retained when w > eps and are excluded from the row sum otherwise. The default of 0 is deliberate: computing the statistic without discarding low weights is the point of the method, and is what distinguishes it from approaches that filter low kernel density estimates first. Raising eps is supported but changes the estimand.

nan_policy

character, how to report a bandwidth at which some cell has no neighbours carrying weight. "zero" (default) reproduces the reference implementation, which reports 0 for the whole affected bandwidth; "drop" excludes only the isolated cells; "na" reports NA so the situation cannot pass unnoticed. All three warn.

moments

logical, compute the exact analytical moments of the permutation null (default TRUE). These cost O(N) per bandwidth on top of work already done, so they are essentially free, and they are exact rather than estimated: the statistic is a linear permutation statistic, whose moments have closed forms. They enable method = "moment" in compute_significance and populate leverage, which reports whether a continuous approximation to the null is trustworthy at each bandwidth.

permute

character, how much permuting to do. "all" (default) permutes at every bandwidth. "flagged" permutes only where the moment diagnostics say a continuous approximation cannot be trusted, using the exact moments elsewhere; this is what turns permutations from the bulk cost into a targeted safety net. "none" skips them entirely and forces perms = 0.

batch_size

integer permutations contracted per batch (default: 256). Bounds peak memory at N x batch_size instead of N x perms; results are unaffected.

n_threads

integer number of threads for the kernel sweep (default: 0, meaning all available). Ignored when the package was built without OpenMP, which includes builds using stock Apple clang.

verbose

logical show progress (default: NULL = auto for large datasets)

large_mode_n

deprecated and ignored. It previously claimed to select a sparse code path, but the threshold was hard-coded in C++ and this argument was never read. There is now a single compute path whose working memory is O(N x length(h)) regardless of N, so no threshold is needed.

kernel

character or function. Built-in options are "gaussian" (the default, and the one the manuscript uses), "uniform" and "exponential". If a function, a custom kernel with signature kernel(dist_matrix, h, ...) returning an N x N weight matrix.

distance

character or function. Built-in options are "euclidean" (default), "manhattan" and "minkowski"; the last takes its order from p. If a function, a custom distance with signature distance(coords, ...) returning an N x N distance matrix.

Value

An S4 object of class kernelcomm_result with slots:

h

numeric vector of bandwidth values used

observed

numeric vector of Moran's I for each bandwidth

permutations

numeric matrix (n_h x perms) of permuted I values

coords

matrix of original coordinates

gene1_name

character. Name of gene 1

gene2_name

character. Name of gene 2

sample_id

character. Sample identifier

seed

numeric. Random seed used

n_cells

integer. Number of cells

call

language. Function call that created this object

p_values, z_scores, perm_mean, perm_sd, null_lower, null_upper, significant, p_adjusted

NULL (computed by compute_significance)

Details

Built-in Kernels:

  • "gaussian": \(w_{ij} = \exp(-d_{ij}^2 / (2h^2))\). The default, and the kernel the manuscript uses. Unbounded support, so every pair contributes.

  • "uniform": \(w_{ij} = 1\) if \(d_{ij} \le h\), else 0. A hard radius, so cells can genuinely have no neighbours; see nan_policy.

  • "exponential": \(w_{ij} = \exp(-d_{ij} / h)\). Note the shape relative to the Gaussian, because the intuitive reading is wrong: it is smaller than \(\exp(-d^2/2h^2)\) for \(d < 2h\) and larger only beyond, crossing over at exactly \(d = 2h\). So it decays faster near the origin and has the heavier tail further out, and because the near field dominates the row sum, a given h gives a smaller effective neighbourhood than the Gaussian rather than a larger one.

The diagonal is always zero: a cell is not its own neighbour, which for single cells is not a meaningful notion. Row sums are normalised to 1, so \(I(h)\) stays bounded and every cell contributes equally regardless of local density.

Built-in Distance Methods:

  • "euclidean": \(\sqrt{(x_i - x_j)^2 + (y_i - y_j)^2}\)

  • "manhattan": \(|x_i - x_j| + |y_i - y_j|\)

  • "minkowski": \((|x_i - x_j|^p + |y_i - y_j|^p)^{1/p}\), with p passed through .... p = 1 and p = 2 are routed to the Manhattan and Euclidean paths, which compute the same thing without calling pow().

All combinations run inside the same tiled core, so none of them can bypass the eps predicate or the zero-row-sum policy. Only a user-supplied function takes the R fallback path.

Custom Kernel Functions: Custom kernel functions must have signature: kernel(dist_matrix, h, ...) where:

  • dist_matrix: N x N matrix of pairwise distances

  • h: scalar bandwidth for current computation

  • ...: additional parameters passed from multiScaleAC

The function must return an N x N weight matrix (can be dense matrix or sparse Matrix::dsCMatrix).

Custom Distance Functions: Custom distance functions must have signature: distance(coords, ...) where:

  • coords: N x 2 matrix of coordinates

  • ...: additional parameters (e.g., p for Minkowski distance)

The function must return an N x N distance matrix.

Choosing bandwidths: Bandwidths are in the units of coords. This is the most common source of meaningless results. If h is far too large, every pairwise weight approaches 1, the kernel becomes a constant matrix, and \(I(h)\) collapses toward zero for every gene pair; if far too small, no cell has a neighbour carrying weight and the statistic is undefined. The bundled ccRCCExample data is in millimetres and spans about 1 mm, so bandwidths of roughly 0.01 to 0.25 are appropriate; the same tissue measured in micrometres would want 10 to 250. Use suggest_bandwidths rather than guessing, and qc_neighborhoods to confirm the effective neighbourhood size before interpreting the curve.

Performance: The built-in kernels and distances use a two-pass sweep that computes each pair distance once and reuses it across all bandwidths, with working memory of O(N x length(h)) rather than O(N^2). Custom kernel or distance functions are evaluated in R and do build a full N x N matrix, so they are limited to smaller N.

See also

compute_significance to add p-values, suggest_bandwidths to choose h, multiScaleAC_batch for many samples, soupir_moran_bv for single-bandwidth analysis, and soupir_moran_multi, the reference implementation, which remains supported and is not deprecated.

Examples

# Bandwidths are in coordinate units. These coordinates span the unit square,
# so bandwidths of a few hundredths cover a handful of neighbours each.
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
coords <- matrix(runif(2 * n), ncol = 2)
g1 <- rnorm(n)
g2 <- rnorm(n)

result <- multiScaleAC(coords, g1, g2, h = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2), perms = 99)
result
#> multiScaleAC result
#> ===================
#> Sample: sample1 
#> Gene pair: g1 x g2 
#> Bandwidths: 3 values from 0.05 to 0.2 
#> Permutations: 99 
#> Cells: 200 
#> Significance: Not computed (use compute_significance())

# Check that a bandwidth gives a sensible neighbourhood size before trusting
# the curve: a mean close to N means the kernel is saturated and I(h) will
# collapse toward zero regardless of the biology.
qc_neighborhoods(coords, h = 0.1)
#>     h mean_neighbors sd_neighbors min_neighbors max_neighbors isolated_cells
#> 1 0.1       11.65468      3.47906      1.321834      17.75342              0
#>   percent_isolated saturation
#> 1                0     0.0583

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Custom kernel (exponential decay). Evaluated in R, so N x N memory.
exp_kernel <- function(dist_matrix, h) exp(-dist_matrix / h)
result_custom <- multiScaleAC(coords, g1, g2, h = c(0.05, 0.1),
                              kernel = exp_kernel)

# Custom distance (Minkowski, p = 3) with the default Gaussian kernel.
minkowski_dist <- function(coords, p = 3) {
  as.matrix(dist(coords, method = "minkowski", p = p))
}
result_mink <- multiScaleAC(coords, g1, g2, h = c(0.05, 0.1),
                            distance = minkowski_dist, p = 3)
} # }
